title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary school students and teachers perceived a generative AI-powered learning activity for creative mathematical writing. The authors were interested in both the educational benefits and the challenges of using GenAI to help students create, revise, and reflect on story-based math problems.

The intervention involved a custom GenAI learning platform that supported students through three steps: Ask, Represent, and Transform. In Ask, students analyzed and discussed math stories; in Represent, they visually modeled ideas; and in Transform, they prompted GenAI to co-generate culturally relevant math stories using text and images (GPT-4 and DALL·E 3). Students then evaluated the AI-generated stories and revised their own work. The study was implemented in six 5th-grade classrooms across two U.S. elementary schools, involving 79 students and six teachers. Data came from student focus groups, teacher interviews, open-ended surveys, and classroom observations, and were analyzed thematically.

The study found that participants perceived several benefits: GenAI supported divergent and convergent thinking, helped students understand mathematical concepts and represent knowledge, promoted AI literacy through prompt refinement, and increased interest, curiosity, and ownership of learning. At the same time, students and teachers identified challenges, including weak critical evaluation of AI outputs, difficulty generating coherent prompts and stories, AI being perceived as too perfect, lack of adaptive pedagogical feedback, limited autonomy, weak social connection features, and insufficient accessibility options such as speech-to-text. The authors conclude that GenAI can support creative mathematical writing in elementary classrooms, but only when paired with deliberate instructional and interface design that preserves opportunities for human learning and interaction.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI GPT-based generative AI system used for text generation and related conversational assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used within the developed GenAI-powered learning technology to generate draft mathematical stories from student input; the paper states the system integrated OpenAI’s GPT-4 and DALL·E 3.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative artificial intelligence system that can generate text and images and support content creation, drafting, and feedback-like interaction.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a GenAI-powered classroom technology for creative mathematical writing; students used it to draft, modify, and create culturally relevant math stories and to evaluate AI-generated stories.

findings.finding_summary: Participants reported that GenAI supported creative mathematical writing by fostering creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, and affective engagement. Reported benefits included story generation, visual representation, prompt iteration, and increased interest, curiosity, and ownership, but the study was qualitative and did not estimate causal effects.
findings.measure: Perceived benefits and challenges in interview themes and observation notes

findings.finding_summary: Participants also reported several challenges: students often did not critically evaluate AI-generated content, had difficulty generating coherent prompts/stories, and felt the AI was too perfect. Teachers and students wanted more adaptive feedback, autonomy, social interaction, and multiple communication modes such as speech-to-text.
findings.measure: Perceived barriers and design needs from interviews and triangulated qualitative data

quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative mixed-methods classroom study with interviews, surveys, and observations. It provides useful classroom evidence, but there is no experimental comparison or quantitative effect estimate.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports positive perceived impacts on engagement, creativity, and mathematical understanding, but these are qualitative and not quantified. Because no effect size is reported, the impact tier is best treated as modest/unclear.
